source_refs.note: Chapter 15 exercise (PDF 57-59, printed 13-15), solved: 8 MCQs keyed from the chapter, 9 short and 5 constructed response questions with model answers, 7 numerical problems worked step by step. The book prints no answers.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “Choose the correction answer” is a misprint for Choose the correct answer.

blocks.prompt: 15.1 When the light from two lamps falls on a screen, no interference pattern can be obtained. Why is this?

options.text: The lamps are not point sources.
The lamps emit light of different amplitudes.
The light from the lamps is not coherent.
The light from the lamps is white

blocks.explanation: Interference needs coherent sources (constant phase difference). Two separate lamps emit independent random bursts of light, so their phase difference keeps changing and the pattern changes too fast to see; we see only uniform light.

blocks.prompt: 15.2 Monochromatic light illuminates two narrow parallel slits. The interference pattern which results is observed on a screen some distance beyond the slits. Which change increases the separation between the dark lines of the interference pattern?

options.text: Decreasing the distance between the screen and the slits
Increasing the distance between the slits
Using monochromatic light of longer wavelength

blocks.explanation: Fringe spacing Δy = Lλ/d. A longer wavelength increases Δy. Decreasing L, increasing d or using higher frequency (shorter λ) all make the fringes closer.

blocks.prompt: 15.3 Using monochromatic light, interference fringes are produced on a screen placed a distance L from a pair of slits of separation d. The separation of the fringes is y. Both d and L are now doubled. What is the new fringe separation?
blocks.explanation: Δy = Lλ/d. New spacing = (2L)λ/(2d) = Lλ/d = y, so the spacing does not change.

blocks.prompt: 15.4 Which of the following is not a necessary condition for two waves to produce interference.

options.text: Waves must be of same type
Waves must be moving in same direction

blocks.explanation: The chapter lists the conditions: same type of waves, coherent waves, moving in the same or almost same direction. Waves of different amplitudes still interfere; only the contrast of the pattern decreases.

blocks.prompt: 15.5 The colours appeared on a soap bubble are due to which phenomenon of light?
blocks.explanation: Light reflected from the front and back surfaces of the thin soap film interferes; different wavelengths reinforce at different thicknesses, giving colours (15.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is printed “Interference is this film”; it means interference in thin film.

blocks.prompt: 15.6 Continuous water waves are diffracted through a gap in a barrier in a ripple tank. Which change will cause the diffraction of the waves to increase?

options.text: Increasing the frequency of the waves
Increasing the width of the gap
Reducing the wavelength of the waves
Reducing the width of the gap

blocks.explanation: Diffraction (spreading) is greatest when the gap is comparable to the wavelength. Reducing the gap width increases spreading; increasing frequency or reducing wavelength decreases it.

blocks.prompt: 15.7 Which property of a light wave can be determined using a diffraction grating?
blocks.explanation: From d sin θ = nλ, measuring the angle θ of an order n with a known grating spacing d gives the wavelength λ very precisely.

blocks.prompt: 15.8 The central maximum in a diffraction grating is called:
blocks.explanation: The central maximum is at θ = 0, so d sin θ = nλ gives n = 0: it is the zero order.

blocks.prompt: 15.1 Can Huygens' Principle be applied on sound and water waves? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: Yes. Huygens' principle is a geometrical method for any wave: every point of a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets moving with the wave's speed, and their envelope is the new wavefront. Sound and water waves also have wavefronts, so their spreading, reflection, refraction and diffraction can be explained with it.

blocks.prompt: 15.2 Why interference pattern is produced due to headlights of a car? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: Actually no interference pattern is produced. The two headlights are independent sources: they are not coherent (their phase difference changes randomly and rapidly) and they emit many wavelengths. So the pattern, if any, changes too fast to be seen and we see only uniform illumination.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question as printed asks why an interference pattern IS produced by car headlights. No such pattern is produced: the two headlights are incoherent sources. The question should read 'Why is no interference pattern produced…'; the answer above explains this.

blocks.prompt: 15.3 Why interference pattern is observed on soap bubbles but not on window glass or windscreens of cars?
blocks.explanation: A soap film is very thin (thickness comparable to the wavelength of light), so the path difference between light reflected from its front and back surfaces is a few wavelengths and different colours reinforce at different places. Window glass and windscreens are millimetres thick; the path difference is thousands of wavelengths, the fringes of all colours overlap and are far too close, so no pattern is seen.

blocks.prompt: 15.4 If the whole apparatus of Young's double slit experiment is submerged in water, what will be the effect on fringes?
blocks.explanation: In water the wavelength of light becomes λw = λ/n (n ≈ 1.33). Since Δy = Lλ/d, the fringe width decreases by the factor n (to about 3/4 of its value in air). The fringes come closer together; the central fringe stays bright.

blocks.prompt: 15.5 Compare the Double slit experimental arrangements for light and sound waves, similarities and differences.
blocks.explanation: Both are two-source interference experiments: both need coherent sources of the same wavelength; maxima are where the path difference is mλ and minima where it is (m + ½)λ; Δy = Lλ/d applies to both.

rows: Coherence: one laser beam divided by two slits
Coherence: two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator
Slit separation: a fraction of a millimetre
Speaker separation: about a metre (λ is centimetres to metres)
Detected by ear or a microphone moved across the region

blocks.prompt: 15.6 For a diffraction grating, what are the advantages of using (a) many slits, (b) narrow slits and (c) closely spaced slits? Explain
blocks.explanation:
(a) Many slits: the maxima become very sharp, narrow and bright, so their angles and hence wavelengths are measured very precisely.
(b) Narrow slits: each slit diffracts (spreads) light more widely, so light reaches large angles and higher orders can be seen.
(c) Closely spaced slits (small d): from sin θ = nλ/d the orders lie at larger angles and are more widely separated, so the spectrum spreads out more and is easier to measure.

blocks.prompt: 15.7 How the number of orders in a given diffraction grating can be increased?
blocks.explanation: From d sin θ = nλ and sin θ ≤ 1, the highest order is n(max) = d/λ (whole-number part). So the number of orders increases by using a grating with larger spacing d (fewer lines per mm) or light of shorter wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 15.8 Explain how the pattern would change if red light is replaced with blue light in a given diffraction grating?
blocks.explanation: Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red. From sin θ = nλ/d, each order of blue appears at a smaller angle, nearer to the central maximum, so the lines come closer together (less spread). The central maximum (n = 0) stays at θ = 0, and more orders may be visible since n(max) = d/λ increases.

blocks.prompt: 15.9 Why central spot in Newton's rings is dark?
blocks.explanation: At the centre the lens touches the glass plate, so the air film thickness and the geometrical path difference are zero. But light reflected from the lower (air-to-glass) surface undergoes a half-cycle (λ/2) phase shift. The two reflected waves are therefore in antiphase and interfere destructively, so the centre is dark.

blocks.prompt: 15.1 Light sometimes describes as rays and sometimes as waves. Construct diagrams to explain differences in both.
blocks.explanation:
Ray diagram: draw light as straight lines with arrowheads showing the direction of travel, e.g. a ray striking a plane mirror and reflecting with angle i = angle r, or parallel rays passing through a convex lens and meeting at its focus. Rays explain straight-line travel, shadows, reflection and refraction (geometrical optics).
Wave diagram: draw a series of wavefronts (parallel lines for a plane wave, circles for a point source) one wavelength λ apart, with a ray arrow drawn perpendicular to them. At a narrow gap, draw the wavefronts curving out beyond it (Huygens' wavelets). Waves explain interference, diffraction and the bending of light into the geometrical shadow.
A ray is the direction of travel of energy and is always perpendicular to the wavefronts.

rows: Light shown as straight lines with arrows
Light shown as wavefronts (lines or circles) one λ apart
Shows only the direction of travel of light
Shows phase, wavelength and how the wave spreads
Explains rectilinear propagation, shadows, reflection, refraction
Explains interference, diffraction (and also reflection, refraction)
Cannot explain fringes or bending into the shadow
Gives fringes and spreading through narrow slits

blocks.prompt: 15.2 Suppose white light is falling on a double slit arrangement, such that one slit is covered with red filter (400 nm) and other is with blue filter (650 nm), explain what would be observed on the screen?
blocks.explanation: The two slits now send light of different wavelengths (red and blue), so the two sources have different frequencies and are not coherent; there is no constant phase difference. Hence no steady interference fringes are formed. The screen shows the red and blue light from the two slits overlapping, a fairly uniform patch of mixed (magenta/purple) colour, each colour only spread out by diffraction at its own slit.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints red filter (400 nm) and blue filter (650 nm). The wavelengths are swapped: red light is about 650 nm and blue about 400-450 nm. The answer does not change: the two slits give light of different wavelengths, so no interference fringes form.

blocks.prompt: 15.3 What will be the effect on width and brightness of the fringes in a double slit interference experiment if we decrease the width of one slit to half keeping all other thing same?
blocks.explanation:
Width: fringe width Δy = Lλ/d does not depend on slit width, so the fringe width remains the same.
Brightness: the narrower slit passes half the light, so its wave has a smaller amplitude (about A/√2). Amplitudes are no longer equal, so:
- bright fringes become less bright: (A + 0.71A)² ≈ 2.9A² instead of 4A²;
- dark fringes are no longer completely dark: (A − 0.71A)² ≈ 0.09A² instead of 0.
The contrast between bright and dark fringes decreases (the chapter: unequal amplitudes decrease the contrast).

blocks.prompt: 15.4 Why can we readily observe diffraction effects for sound wave and water waves, but not for light? Is this because light travels so much faster than these other waves? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Diffraction is noticeable only when the size of the gap or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength. Sound waves (λ from about 2 cm to 17 m) and water waves (centimetres to metres) have wavelengths similar to doors, windows and gaps around us, so they bend a lot. Light has λ of only 400-700 nm, far smaller than everyday openings, so its bending is tiny and needs very narrow slits to be seen.
It is not because light is faster. Diffraction depends on λ compared with the opening, not on the speed. Light is fast, but its frequency is so high that λ = v/f is very small.

blocks.prompt: 15.5 What is the significance of path difference in deriving Bragg's equation?
blocks.explanation:
In Bragg's derivation X-rays are reflected from successive parallel atomic planes a distance d apart. The ray reflected from the lower plane travels an extra distance d sin θ going in and d sin θ coming out, so the path difference = 2d sin θ.
A strong reflected beam appears only when the reflected rays reinforce, i.e. when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: 2d sin θ = nλ (Bragg's equation).
So the path difference links the measurable angle θ and wavelength λ to the interplanar spacing d; it explains why reflection occurs only at certain angles and lets us find the crystal spacing (and structure) from the angle.

blocks.prompt: 15.1 Coherent light of wavelength 500 nm is incident on two very narrow and closely spaced slits. The interference pattern is observed on a very tall screen that is 2.00 m from the slits. Near the center of the screen the separation between two adjacent interference maxima is 3.53 cm. What is the distance on the screen between the m = 49 and m = 50 maxima?
blocks.explanation:
Given: λ = 500 nm = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m, L = 2.00 m, Δy (near the centre) = 3.53 cm = 3.53 × 10⁻² m
Required: y₅₀ − y₄₉
Step 1 (slit separation): Δy = Lλ/d, so d = Lλ/Δy = (2.00 m × 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m)/(3.53 × 10⁻² m) = 2.83 × 10⁻⁵ m
Step 2: for m = 49 and 50 the angles are large, so y = Lλm/d cannot be used; use d sin θ = mλ and y = L tan θ (Eq. 15.3).
m = 49: sin θ₄₉ = 49λ/d = 49 × 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ / 2.83 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.865, θ₄₉ = 59.9°
y₄₉ = L tan θ₄₉ = 2.00 m × tan 59.9° = 3.45 m
m = 50: sin θ₅₀ = 50λ/d = 0.883, θ₅₀ = 61.9°
y₅₀ = 2.00 m × tan 61.9° = 3.75 m
Step 3: y₅₀ − y₄₉ = 3.75 m − 3.45 m = 0.307 m
Answer: about 30.7 cm (much larger than 3.53 cm, because the small-angle formula fails far from the centre).

blocks.prompt: 15.2 Young's experiment is performed with light from excited helium atoms λ = 502 nm. Fringes are measured carefully on a screen 1.20 m away from the double slit, and the center of the 20th fringe (not counting the central bright fringe) is found to be 10.6 mm from the center of the central bright fringe. What is the separation of the two slits?
blocks.explanation:
Given: λ = 502 nm = 5.02 × 10⁻⁷ m, L = 1.20 m, m = 20, y₂₀ = 10.6 mm = 1.06 × 10⁻² m
Required: slit separation d
Formula: yₘ = mLλ/d, so d = mLλ/yₘ
d = (20 × 1.20 m × 5.02 × 10⁻⁷ m)/(1.06 × 10⁻² m)
d = (1.205 × 10⁻⁵ m²)/(1.06 × 10⁻² m) = 1.14 × 10⁻³ m
Answer: d = 1.14 mm

blocks.prompt: 15.3 Coherent light with wavelength 450 nm falls on a pair of slits. On a screen 1.80 m away, the distance between dark fringes is 3.90 mm. What is the slit separation?
blocks.explanation:
Given: λ = 450 nm = 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m, L = 1.80 m, distance between dark fringes Δy = 3.90 mm = 3.90 × 10⁻³ m
Required: slit separation d
Adjacent dark fringes are separated by the same Δy as bright fringes: Δy = Lλ/d, so d = Lλ/Δy
d = (1.80 m × 4.50 × 10⁻⁷ m)/(3.90 × 10⁻³ m)
d = (8.10 × 10⁻⁷ m²)/(3.90 × 10⁻³ m) = 2.08 × 10⁻⁴ m
Answer: d = 0.208 mm

blocks.prompt: 15.4 Two slits spaced 0.450 mm apart are placed 75.0 cm from a screen. What is the distance between the second and third dark lines of the interference pattern on the screen when the slits are illuminated with coherent light with a wavelength of 500 nm?
blocks.explanation:
Given: d = 0.450 mm = 4.50 × 10⁻⁴ m, L = 75.0 cm = 0.750 m, λ = 500 nm = 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m
Required: distance between the 2nd and 3rd dark lines
Adjacent dark lines (d sin θ = (m + ½)λ) are one fringe width apart: Δy = Lλ/d
Δy = (0.750 m × 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ m)/(4.50 × 10⁻⁴ m)
Δy = (3.75 × 10⁻⁷ m²)/(4.50 × 10⁻⁴ m) = 8.33 × 10⁻⁴ m
Answer: 0.833 mm

blocks.prompt: 15.5 Two very narrow slits are spaced 1.80 mm apart and are placed 35.0 cm from a screen. What is the distance between the first and second dark lines of the interference pattern when the slits are illuminated with coherent light of wavelength 550 nm?
blocks.explanation:
Given: d = 1.80 mm = 1.80 × 10⁻³ m, L = 35.0 cm = 0.350 m, λ = 550 nm = 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m
Required: distance between the 1st and 2nd dark lines
Adjacent dark lines are one fringe width apart: Δy = Lλ/d
Δy = (0.350 m × 5.50 × 10⁻⁷ m)/(1.80 × 10⁻³ m)
Δy = (1.925 × 10⁻⁷ m²)/(1.80 × 10⁻³ m) = 1.07 × 10⁻⁴ m
Answer: 0.107 mm

blocks.prompt: 15.6 Monochromatic light is at normal incidence on a plane transmission grating. The first-order maximum in the interference pattern is at an angle of 11.3o. What is the angular position of the fourth-order maximum?
blocks.explanation:
Given: n = 1 at θ₁ = 11.3°; required θ₄ for n = 4
Formula: d sin θ = nλ
For n = 1: sin θ₁ = λ/d = sin 11.3° = 0.196
For n = 4: sin θ₄ = 4λ/d = 4 × 0.196 = 0.784
θ₄ = sin⁻¹(0.784) = 51.6°
Answer: the fourth-order maximum is at 51.6° (not 4 × 11.3°, because sin θ, not θ, is proportional to n).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The angle is printed “11.3o”; it is 11.3°.

blocks.prompt: 15.7 If a diffraction grating produces a third-order bright spot for red light of wavelength 700 nm at 65° from the central maximum, at what angle will the second-order bright spot be for violet light of wavelength 400 nm?
blocks.explanation:
Given: red: n = 3, λ = 700 nm = 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ m, θ = 65°; violet: n = 2, λ = 400 nm = 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ m
Required: angle θ for the violet second order
Step 1 (grating spacing): d sin θ = nλ, so d = nλ/sin θ = (3 × 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ m)/sin 65° = (2.10 × 10⁻⁶ m)/0.906 = 2.32 × 10⁻⁶ m
Step 2: sin θ = nλ/d = (2 × 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ m)/(2.32 × 10⁻⁶ m) = 0.345
θ = sin⁻¹(0.345) = 20.2°
Answer: about 20.2° from the central maximum.
